project.title: Serendipity at the tool crib (example walk)

brief.researchQuestion: You expected that Dave's walking founders over to each other was what produced the useful leads, and that "most of his reasons to walk round the bench went with the whiteboard", yet you also "didn't expect the useful leads to go to the helpers" or founders to describe the booking system "only as a gain". Your February fieldnote has Dave at the whiteboard while Tom and the lidar founder got onto the cable supplier in the queue, and Tom still says "Dave hooked me up with the cable people".
brief.context: I wanted to study the tool crib at this deep-tech incubator because it's the one room where founders from different ventures meet without anyone arranging it. Until May, founders queued for the machines and fixed things at the shared bench while they waited, and the technician, Dave, ran the room with a whiteboard and regularly walked founders over to each other. I watched him introduce a robotics founder to a materials founder in my second week, and the introduction ended with the materials founder's first outside customer, although I noticed only later that Dave made introductions like that one most weeks. Since the online booking system arrived in May, Dave mostly sits at the screen on the front desk, and I've seen perhaps two introductions, both on days that the laser cutter broke down. I think most of his reasons to walk round the bench went with the whiteboard.
brief.siteRationale: I think the incubator is the right place, partly because I have access to it and partly because the crib changed in May while the ventures, the room and Dave stayed the same, which gives me something close to a before and after. I've had a desk there two days a week for eight months, with the programme director's permission and consent from the founders that I've interviewed. At the crib I'll miss the leads that founders pick up elsewhere, in the kitchen or on Slack, because I watch encounters at the bench and don't sit by the kettle, so I'd find those leads only through interviews. I suspect that some serendipity has moved to the kitchen and to Slack, and I could mistake that shift for a loss if I study the crib alone. Of the five runs that I have since May, two started elsewhere (one on Slack and one in the kitchen) and three started at the bench.
brief.processOfInterest: The process that I follow starts at the bench, once a founder brings a problem to the crib, their own or somebody else's. A run ends once somebody acts on a lead that they picked up there, or once the founder leaves with the problem and little else. The time at the bench can be ten minutes, but the acting often comes days or weeks later, so one run can stretch over a fortnight or more. I can watch the start at the bench, but I usually hear about the end second-hand. Priya's complaint about her cell supplier ended a fortnight later with the water-sensing founder switching to her new supplier, and Dave's introduction over the gearbox housing ended three weeks later with a first order for twenty housings.
brief.outcomeOfInterest: I care about whether a chance encounter at the crib turns into a lead that a founder acts on, such as a switched supplier, an order or a borrowed fix. The project would be worth doing if founders who leave with leads like those differ from founders who leave with only their own repair done, and if the number of leads that founders act on falls after the booking system arrived in May. I have evidence outside one founder's own story, a box from the new supplier on his desk and his Slack update about the cold-weather failures, but I'll be relying on founders' accounts for most runs. I count fourteen acted-on leads in my notes from the four months before May and five from the four months since. Since I kept notes differently in the two periods, by the queue before May and in interviews after it, I'm not sure that the counts are comparable.
brief.bind: The founders that I'm studying feel a pull between using their time well and staying available to other founders. The booking system lets them plan their week, which every founder that I've interviewed values, whereas the old queue made them wait around, and the helping happened during the waiting. I think the helpers feel the pull most, because they give up time for someone else's problem with little to show for it until a lead turns up, and Dave feels it too, since the programme director now judges him on machine hours. Priya now does "drive-by help" because the next booking starts on the hour, and she said that the calendar had made her a worse neighbour. In September a robotics founder showed a first-time founder the focus setting for acrylic in two minutes and went back to her cut, saying that she'd have stayed longer "if it wasn't my slot", so her own booking won.
brief.sampleRationale: I need runs from before and after May, and I need both founders who come to help and founders who come for their own repairs in each period, so that I can tell the two comparisons apart. I'd also want some range across the machines, since the laser cutter and the oscilloscopes sit at opposite ends of the room and draw different founders. So far I have eleven interviews and about thirty fieldnotes, but most of the fieldnotes come from before May and most of the interviews from after it. Seven founders appear in both periods, and I can tell their role on most visits for five of them from my fieldnotes, so I'd want to add fieldnotes after May for those seven. My sample after May leans on newcomers who come for their own repairs, while my sample before May leans on old hands who help, so I'd be comparing different founders as much as different periods.
brief.earlySurprise: My material so far is eleven interview transcripts, about thirty fieldnotes from my days at the bench, and a few memos, including one on the booking system. I didn't expect the useful leads to go to the helpers, who came to the crib for other people's problems, and I didn't expect the founders to describe the booking system only as a gain, when I count fewer encounters in my notes after May. Several founders also bring Dave into their account of a lead, and Tom, a sensor founder, told me that "Dave hooked me up with the cable people", although in my February fieldnote Dave stands at the whiteboard all afternoon while Tom and the lidar founder get onto the cable supplier in the queue. So Dave may be getting credit for encounters that happened in the queue without him, or founders may remember an introduction better than a stranger. I can't yet tell those two readings apart.
brief.startingInterest: I'm a third-year PhD student, and I've spent two days a week for the past eight months at a desk in a deep-tech incubator, where founders from different ventures share a tool workshop that everyone calls the tool crib. They queue, borrow tools, fix each other's kit and talk, and a surprising number of the useful leads that founders have told me about started at that bench. I'm interested in serendipity, and in particular in the way that founders notice a chance encounter and then act on it. The crib gives me a small, bounded place where I can watch those encounters happen or fail to happen.

brief.puzzleAnswer: I can't yet explain two things. First, the founders who report the most useful chance encounters are the ones who come to the crib to fix other people's problems, like Priya with the motor controller, while founders who come for their own repairs, like the lidar founder with his headphones on, mostly leave with only the repair. I expected the reverse, because the serendipity literature leads me to expect that a prepared mind finds the leads that it's looking for, and my sense now is that helpers find leads because explaining a fault to another founder means reaching for their own stories. Second, the booking system seems to have cut the encounters down, and yet the founders and the staff talk about the change only as a gain, as Dave did when he called the crib "calmer". I don't know whether the system really cut the encounters or whether my own attention changed after May, when I started interviewing and stopped keeping the oscilloscope list.

Interview with Tom (sensor venture), 2 September 2026, in a meeting room on the first floor, 47 minutes. This excerpt is my transcription of the recording. I is me, and T is Tom.

I: You mentioned the cable supplier earlier. Can you tell me the story of that supplier?

T: Dave hooked me up with the cable people, Dave knows everyone. That was back in February, when our connectors kept failing in the field and I was going through suppliers like crisps. I mentioned it at the crib, and I had samples a week later from a firm in Leeds that I still use.

I: Do you remember the afternoon itself, at the crib?

T: Not really. I remember feeling cross about the crimp tool, because somebody had it signed out and I had to wait. I think I was chatting to Kai from the lidar team about connectors while we waited, and then at some point Dave gave me the name. Or maybe Kai gave me the name and Dave confirmed it. Honestly, Dave is the person that I'd thank.

I: Can you say a bit more about Dave?

T: Dave's the reason that anyone talks to anyone in that room. He'd see two people with the same problem and push them together. If I had a problem in February, I went to the crib, because I knew that Dave would find somebody for me.

I: And now?

T: Now I post on Slack. Since the booking system came in, the crib is a place that you go to for a machine. I'm in and out in my slot, and Dave is at the desk sorting out double bookings, so the crib is quiet. Quiet is good for work, but I don't hear about other teams' problems any more.

I: Can you think of a lead that came to you through Slack?

T: In August I posted about a noisy power rail on our new board, and Mei from the team next door answered within ten minutes and came over that afternoon. We fixed the rail together in about an hour. So Slack works, but it works for the problem that I post. I wouldn't post about a supplier that I'm only half unhappy with, and at the crib that half-unhappiness used to come out in conversation.

I: When you're at the crib now, do you help other people?

T: If they ask. Last week a new founder asked me to show him the settings on the laser cutter, and I did, but my slot was running, so I pointed him at the card on the wall. Before the summer I'd have stayed with him, because we'd both have been waiting anyway.

I: Did the incubator ask the founders about the booking system before it came in?

T: The incubator ran a survey, I think, about waiting times. Everyone hated the queue, so everyone said yes. I said yes too. The incubator asked us about time in the survey, and I don't remember a question about the conversations, and I doubt that I'd have thought of them.

I: Do you ever go to the crib without a booking?

T: Sometimes, to borrow a hand tool. The hand tools don't need a booking, so I go in, sign the tool out on the sheet and leave. If somebody's at the bench I'll say hello, but I don't stay, because I'm not waiting for anything. I was always waiting for something before the summer, so I was always there, and I heard everything that went on at the bench.

I: If the incubator dropped the booking system tomorrow, would you want the queue back?

T: Probably not. I'd want the bookings, and I'd want Dave walking round again. Maybe the answer is to keep the bookings and give Dave his afternoons back. But that's a question for the programme director, and I'm not sure that she sees the crib as a place for meeting people.

I: You said earlier that Kai might have given you the name. Have you talked to Kai about the cable supplier since?

T: Funny you should ask. Kai uses the same firm, and I always assumed that Dave had sent him there too. I haven't asked him yet. Maybe I should, now that you mention it.

End of excerpt.

Fieldnote, Tuesday 22 September 2026, the tool crib, 13:30 to 17:00. I wrote these notes at the bench and typed them up that evening.

I arrive at half past one and take the stool by the oscilloscopes, which I haven't used much since I stopped keeping the list in May. Dave is at the booking screen on the front desk. The laser cutter has a red fault light, and Dave has taped a note in his own handwriting to its lid: "Down until the engineer comes, sorry."

By two o'clock four founders stand by the cutter, all with bookings for the afternoon. Mei from the sensor team has a tray of acrylic panels, Kai from the lidar team has a box of mounts, and two founders whom I don't know yet, from a robotics venture that joined in July, carry a laptop with their cut files. Dave comes over twice to say that the engineer is on her way.

Within twenty minutes the four of them are talking about each other's work. Kai asks the robotics pair about their mounts, because their files look like his, and it turns out that both teams cut brackets for the same lidar unit. Kai shows them a crack that he found in his first version, on the inside corner, and he tells them to add a fillet. One of the robotics founders photographs Kai's bracket with her phone.

Mei asks Dave whether he knows anyone who does conformal coating. Dave says, "Ask Priya, she had a whole saga with it," and then he goes back to the desk, because his screen beeps. Mei messages Priya on Slack without leaving the cutter, and Priya replies within a few minutes with the name of a firm.

The engineer arrives at about three and opens up the cutter. The founders stay, because each of them wants the first slot once the cutter works, and Dave starts to rearrange the afternoon's bookings on his screen. Kai and the robotics pair go over to the bench and lay their brackets side by side. I hear Kai say that he buys his bolts from a firm in Sheffield, and one of the robotics founders writes the name on the back of her hand.

The engineer finishes at twenty past four. Dave gives the first slot to Mei, because her booking was the earliest, and the others drift back to their desks. Kai leaves without cutting, since his slot has gone, and he says to me on his way out, "Worst afternoon this month, and I've learned more than in the whole of August."

Reflection. This afternoon looked like the crib before May, and the difference was the breakdown. The four founders came for their own cuts, and they ended up helping each other because the cutter stopped and the bookings stopped with it. So I wonder whether the booking system cut the encounters directly, or whether it cut the waiting, and the encounters went with the waiting. I also notice that Dave made one introduction today, by name, and he made it from the desk, without walking anyone anywhere. Mei got Priya's firm through Slack, so the introduction worked, although the story behind Priya's saga stayed with Priya.

Memo: the booking system, 25 September 2026

The programme director introduced the online booking system on 6 May for the big machines in the crib: the laser cutter, the 3D printer, the reflow oven and the two oscilloscopes. Before then, founders queued, and Dave kept the order on his whiteboard. Founders now book slots of thirty minutes to two hours, up to a week ahead, and Dave sees an overrun in red on his screen.

So far I count fourteen runs that ended in an acted-on lead in the four months before May, and five in the four months since. I don't trust the comparison yet, for two reasons. First, I sat by the queue most Tuesdays before May, while I've spent more of my days in interviews since then, so I may simply be seeing less. Second, my sample after May leans on newcomers who come for their own repairs, whereas my sample before May leans on old hands who help.

Even so, three observations push me toward a real effect. First, founders now arrive for a slot and leave when it ends, so the waiting has gone, and in my notes the helping happened during the waiting. Second, Dave spends his afternoons at the screen, and he has stopped walking round the bench. Third, on the two days that the laser cutter broke down, the encounters came back.

The puzzle for me is that the founders and the staff describe the change only as a gain. Dave calls the crib "calmer", and Priya calls the booking system "a really good change". My working idea is that the incubator designed the booking system to cut the waiting, and the encounters were a by-product of the waiting that the incubator didn't count. I need fieldnotes after May on the seven founders who span both periods before I can say more.

Interview with Priya (battery venture), 14 August 2026, in the incubator kitchen, 52 minutes. This excerpt is my transcription of the recording. I is me, and P is Priya.

I: Can you tell me about the last time that you were in the crib?

P: Tuesday, I think. I had the reflow oven booked from two till four, so I came in at five to two, ran my boards and left at about ten past four. On my way in, Sam from the robotics team waved me over, because his motor driver was throwing a fault again, and I had a quick look. I'd call it drive-by help. I looked at his scope trace for maybe five minutes and told him to check his ground, and then I had to go, because my slot had started.

I: Is that different from the way that you helped people before the summer?

P: Very different. Before the booking system, you just turned up and waited, and while you waited you ended up in other people's problems. I'd go in for the oscilloscope and stay for an hour, and half of that hour went on somebody else's board. The motor controller in March is the one that I think about, because I went in to help Sam and came out having fixed the water-sensing team's cold-weather problem as well.

I: Can you take me through that afternoon?

P: I was explaining Sam's fault to him, and the easiest way to explain it was my own disaster with a cell batch that died below freezing. Arun from the water team sat on the stool next to us, waiting for the scope, and he turned round and asked for my supplier. I gave him the name on a sticky note. He told me a fortnight later that his units had survived a night at minus eight.

I: Would you have told that story if you'd been at the bench for your own repair?

P: Probably not. When it's my own board, I put my headphones on and get on with it. When I'm helping, I talk the whole time, because I have to explain my reasoning to somebody who didn't ask for a lecture, and my reasoning is mostly my old mistakes. So helping makes me tell stories, and other people overhear the stories.

I: Do you still help people in the way that you did in March?

P: Less. I still look at people's boards, but I don't stay. The next booking starts on the hour, and Dave sees a red bar on his screen if you overrun, so everyone watches the clock. I felt bad about Sam on Tuesday, honestly. I think the calendar has made me a worse neighbour. (She laughs.)

I: Do you think that the booking system has changed the encounters at the crib?

P: I hadn't thought about it like that. The booking system is a really good change, because I can plan my week around the oven, and before it I lost whole afternoons in the queue. I suppose some of those lost afternoons were useful, since Arun's supplier came out of one of them. But I couldn't have told you that in May, because a lost afternoon doesn't feel useful while you're losing it.

I: Do you meet other founders somewhere else now?

P: The kitchen, mostly, and the Slack channel. People post when they're stuck, and I reply if I know the answer. Slack is fine for a quick answer, but it's bad for stories, because people don't write stories in Slack. They write the question, and you answer the question, and that's the end of it.

I: Is there anything that you miss about the queue?

P: Dave, a bit. He used to walk round with his whiteboard pen and say, "You two should talk," and you'd end up talking. Now he sits at the screen and sorts out bookings. I don't blame him, since the programme director counts machine hours now. But the walking round was half of his job, and the incubator didn't replace it with anything.

I: If you could change one thing about the crib, would you?

P: I'd keep the bookings, because I'm not going back to losing afternoons. I'd add an hour on Friday with the machines off, when people could bring problems and Dave could do his walking round. I don't know if anyone would come, though. Founders are busy, and an hour for chatting sounds like a waste until you've had the chat.

I: Is there anything else about the crib that you'd want me to know?

P: Only that I learned most of my supplier list at that bench, from other people's disasters. You can't plan that kind of learning, and it only happens if you're standing there long enough to hear the story.

End of excerpt.

events.text: I'm a third-year PhD student, and for eight months I've spent two days a week at a desk in a deep-tech incubator, where founders from different ventures share a tool workshop called the tool crib. They queue, borrow tools, fix each other's kit and talk, and a surprising number of the useful leads founders have told me about started at that bench. I'm interested in serendipity, particularly in how founders notice a chance encounter and then act on it, and the crib gives me a small, bounded place to watch encounters happen or fail to happen.

On serendipity I lean most on Merton and Barber 2004 and Cunha, Clegg and Mendonça 2010, who treat it as something organisations can make more or less likely. Dew 2009 and de Rond 2014 give me the entrepreneurial side and the argument that serendipity takes work, and Busch 2024 is the most recent attempt to pull the field together. On incubators I draw on Cohen, Bingham and Hallen 2019, who show that accelerators design the contact between founders, which is close to my puzzle.

Your brief has blank fields for the puzzle, the Site rationale and the Sample rationale, so I can't yet see which observation about the tool crib struck you as surprising. From the title and your venue note, I take it that you think the booking system is a design decision with consequences for chance encounters. Published work already covers that claim, and I'd like you to check your puzzle against it before the design settles. From memory (please verify each), the closest findings are Allen (1977) on the effect of physical distance on communication among engineers, Fayard and Weeks (2007) on the effect of the design of photocopier rooms and water coolers on informal interaction, and Catalini (2018) on the effect of lab space's microgeography on the pairing of collaborators. Ingram and Morris (2007) on mixers is a fourth, and it matters because it shows that engineered occasions for mixing often fail to produce mixing. If your puzzle is "scheduled access reduces chance encounters among founders," those accounts already predict it. Your study would then redescribe a known regularity in an incubator, and a reviewer at Organization Science will say so. An expectation-violating version would start from something that you saw and that those accounts can't house. One example is founders who meet more through the booking queue than they would at open access. Another is bookings that produce the encounters that people later call lucky. Do you have an observation of that kind? If you do, put it in the Puzzle field in a sentence or two, along with whose expectation it strains.

On scope, the brief doesn't name actors, periods or counter-sites, so I'm guessing at the exclusions. The likely ones are the incubator staff who designed the booking system, founders who don't use the crib, the period before the system existed, and incubators with open access. My sense is that the pre-booking period and the non-users are doing the silent theoretical work. If you claim that booking changes serendipity, you carry an implicit picture of the period without booking, and the source of that picture is unstated in your design as written. Your two target venues also imply two different casings of the same material. Organization Science reads the crib as an organizational arrangement, and AMJ reads it as a question about founders' attention. Each casing calls up a different literature and makes different features of your material salient, so I'd rather you pick between them deliberately than let the choice of journal settle it later.

You have three options. First, write one paragraph stating what you currently expect to find at the crib and which observation, real or imagined, would contradict you, then see whether the puzzle survives. Second, keep your single site and look for variation inside it: bookings that founders swap, walk-ins that the system tolerates, staff overrides, and any weeks in which the system was down. Those moments give you the "without booking" picture without bolting on a second incubator before you understand your first anomaly. Third, if you accept that the study is descriptive, say so in the brief and name the pre-booking period as a scope condition that you aren't covering. That is a legitimate choice, but it changes which journal fits.

You haven't named the kind of material that the study rests on, and I don't want to assume it. The crib can produce at least three kinds of record. Fieldnotes record the events that you watched. An interview records the account that a founder gave you afterwards. Booking logs, sign-in sheets or incubator emails are records the setting produced for its own purposes. Each answers a different question about serendipity. A log can show the people present at the crib at the same time, but it can't show whether they spoke. A founder's story about a lucky meeting is a rehearsed account, and the founder has probably told it before to investors, to staff or to other visitors. If you later load a passage that the founder rehearsed, the reading that you'd revise most is any claim about the course of the encounter, because you'd be reading the founder's account of the meeting.

This matters for your design because a study about serendipity is especially exposed to retrospective storytelling. Founders tidy lucky encounters into narratives once the encounters have paid off. If your data plan is mostly interviews plus logs, you could end up with strong evidence about co-presence and about the way that people tell the story, and very little about the events at the crib itself. A reviewer will see that gap quickly.

You could do any of these. State the data type in the brief now, source by source, even if you've yet to collect some of it. When you load chunks, tag each as observed, recounted or setting-produced, and ask of every passage the identity of its writer and of the readers that the writer expected. Or add a short run of observation sessions at the crib, timed around slot handovers, so you have at least some material that you observed yourself. Or keep the current plan and treat the study explicitly as a study of the ways that founders account for chance encounters, which is a narrower claim but a defensible one.

Your brief has the Puzzle, Site rationale and Sample rationale fields empty, and you've listed the data type as not stated. I can't audit the novelty of a puzzle that you haven't written down, so I'm working from the one thing that you did say: the crib is an organisational arrangement, the booking system is a design decision that the incubator made, and the paper might end up about founders' attention.

If the puzzle is that a tool crib in an incubator produces chance encounters among founders, I think the closest published findings already answer much of it. As I remember them, Allen's work on proximity and communication in R&D labs (1977) shows that physical arrangement shapes who talks to whom. Catalini's study of a lab relocation (Management Science, 2018) shows that forced co-location changes which collaborations form. Boudreau and colleagues' field experiment on search costs and scientific collaboration (2017) shows that lowering the cost of meeting shifts who partners with whom. Please check my recollection of each against the papers. If these are close to right, a study showing that shared equipment creates unplanned contact would redescribe a known regularity in a new setting. An expectation-violating version would start from the booking system. The Allen-style prediction is that scheduled access suppresses random collision, because people arrive on their own slots and leave. If your crib produces serendipity despite or because of a booking system, that is a puzzle that the literature doesn't answer.

The second is the incubator's decision history for the booking system, which probably lives in management meetings and internal messages. The third is the booking data itself. Who is the named gatekeeper for each, and what have they agreed to in writing or in conversation? "I'll ask the director once I'm there" or "a confidentiality agreement will cover it" is a hope, and closed organisational settings often refuse or curtail observation after the first enthusiastic meeting. Incubators also have founders with confidential products, which gives the director a reason to limit a researcher standing at the crib with a notebook.

This matters for your study because a question about the way that serendipity unfolds is a process question, and the elementary unit is the event: an encounter, a missed encounter, a booking that displaces a conversation (Langley, 1999). You capture events best in real time, and if retrospection is unavoidable, contemporaneous traces have to fix the sequence (Langley et al., 2013). If observation of the crib collapses, you're left with founders telling you afterwards about chance meetings, and accounts of serendipity are especially prone to rehearsal. People tell the story of the lucky encounter in light of the outcome that it produced. At review, that gap would be the first thing that a process-minded reader presses on. Your venue choice adds a second problem. Organization Science and AMJ would want different things from the same material (the crib as an organisational arrangement versus founders' attention), and your access determines which paper is even possible.

I'd also ask you to decide on the kind of record that you're building the study on, since your brief leaves the data type unstated. A booking log is something the setting produced for its own purposes. It records reservations and doesn't record encounters, and the incubator wrote it for administration, so a reading of it as evidence of co-presence would change if it turned out to be a system that people worked around. An interview is something recounted to you. Fieldnotes are something that you observed. Each supports different claims about sequence.

That version would lean toward Organization Science and the design decision, and it may be the more executable paper.

Keep the observation-centred design as it stands, but only if you accept a scope condition: if the gatekeeper hasn't confirmed access to the crib floor by a date that you set, the study becomes the fallback above and the venue conversation with your supervisor follows from that. The first is a measurement artifact. You say that you watch encounters at the bench and don't sit by the kettle, so the three bench-started runs are things that you saw, while you learned of the two runs that started on Slack and in the kitchen through interviews. Those are different kinds of record. A founder recounting where a lead came from is giving you a story with the ending already known, and the kitchen is a plausible origin for almost any lead. If the founders rehearsed those two accounts, or reconstructed them after the run succeeded, your picture of serendipity's location would change, and the bench count would still be the only count that you observed. You haven't selected any data chunks for me, so I can't separate the runs that rest on your own notes from the runs that rest on interview talk, and I'd want you to be able to say that for each of the five.

The second is a sampling accident. Five runs since May, split three and two, is too small to read as a migration. I also don't see a count for before May. You've had the desk for eight months, so you have roughly three months before the change, but the brief doesn't give the number of runs that started in each place in that period, or the method that you used to decide that something counts as a run. Without that baseline, two elsewhere could be the usual rate.

A founder asked about the crib after the change may offer the kitchen and Slack as origins because that answer is gracious, or because serendipity is the story the programme likes to tell about itself. Founders also write Slack posts for the setting's own purposes, and in a post that a founder writes for the channel that you read, you read the message that the founder wanted colleagues to read.

The first is the fieldnotes from after May, which you describe as thin. The second is the fieldnotes on the seven founders who appear in both periods, especially the two whose role you can't tell on most visits. The third is the two runs that started on Slack and in the kitchen, along with any interview talk about them. One question only that material can answer: for each of the seven founders who appear in both periods, what did the person do at the bench before May and after May, helping or repairing their own kit, and what does their post-May interview say about encounters they used to have and no longer do?

So I'm asking you directly. What are you avoiding in that unread portion? A hostile reviewer will go straight there. My guess is that the reviewer will say that you can't separate your helper versus own-repair contrast from old hand versus newcomer and from before versus after, and that the seven are the only group in which you can separate them. The same reviewer will say your claim that the booking system cut encounters rests on a counting instrument that changed in May, when interviews replaced the oscilloscope list. Those are your two puzzles, and I suspect they share one weakness.

This matters because a process claim depends on a credible ordering of events. Langley's guidance is that retrospective accounts compress and rationalize sequence in light of known outcomes, so they need contemporaneous traces to fix what happened [L6]. Your post-May material leans on interviews, and your pre-May material leans on notes written at the bench. You also haven't defined an encounter or a "run", and the process tradition treats that boundary as the elementary specification problem [L3]. May is a good temporal bracket, with continuity inside each period and a discontinuity at the frontier [L4]. A bracket only compares like with like if the same founders and the same kind of record sit on both sides. Two years from now, a reader would check a paper that reports "helpers find more leads" and "the booking system cut encounters" against exactly this gap. You've also been at the crib eight months, and interviewing may have taught founders to narrate encounters as leads, so some runs could come from your presence. Stopping the oscilloscope list was a choice about the entries to record, and it protected something. I'd want you to know the thing that it protected.

I see three ways forward. First, before you read more interviews, build one dated line per founder for the seven, with each visit tagged as helping or own repair, and lay the seven lines side by side as a visual map [L11]. Mark the two founders whose roles you can't read as gaps, not guesses. Second, narrow the claim. You could make the helper argument within one period only, state that the founders that you sampled in each period confound the before and after comparison, and keep the booking-system question as a stated limit. Third, rebuild a contemporaneous trace for the counting problem. Recover the pre-May oscilloscope list and any booking logs, and write a dated note that records the May change in your own practice as an event in the data. If you'd rather keep the design as it is, that's defensible, provided the paper says outright that you can't yet tell the two comparisons apart. Which of the three would you start on tomorrow morning?

events.text:
My concern is with one sentence in your puzzle: "helpers find leads because explaining a fault to another founder means reaching for their own stories." You wrote it without a hedge, and it reads as understanding. If I try to read it as a mechanism, I can't tell the cause from the effect. Does the lead surface while the helper is explaining the fault? Does it come later, from the founder that the helper helps, or from a third person that overhears? Is the lead found by the helper or handed to them? And under what conditions does reaching for a story happen at all? Priya with the motor controller is a good illustration of the claim, but an example is not a mechanism. It shows one visit in which the outcome and the role co-occurred. It doesn't give the order of events that would make the role produce the outcome.

Your Sample rationale makes this harder to leave alone. You say the sample before May leans on old hands who help, and the sample after May leans on newcomers who come for their own repairs. So "helper" may be standing in for tenure, a wider network, or familiarity with Dave. The lidar founder with his headphones on may be a case of closed posture, which would be a different mechanism from "came for his own repair." Your own note that you can tell the role on most visits for only five of the seven founders who appear in both periods suggests the role variable is thinner than the sentence makes it sound.

The fieldnotes questions apply here too. At the bench, you see the founders that talk to each other, but you don't see the story that a helper reaches for in their head. Your account of the stories comes from interviews, after the fact, and founders who helped may narrate a visit as productive because helping gave them a reason to tell it. You also have a desk at the incubator two days a week and a visible habit of interviewing since May. Helpers may be more willing to talk to you than founders with headphones on, which would shape the encounters that you record as useful.

This matters because your surprise is real and worth keeping: you expected the prepared mind to find its own leads, and the data ran the other way. But the sentence resolves the surprise with the first casing that arrived. At review in Organization Science, a reader will ask for the sequence and the conditions, and will see a role contrast confounded with period and tenure. Two years from now, if the claim stays as a feeling, you risk building the booking-system argument on top of it. Alternative casings would predict different things in your notes. If helping gives a founder a legitimate license to approach strangers, leads should appear in the way that the conversation opens. If tenure and tie breadth matter, the same founder should find leads whether helping or not. If headphones and posture matter, role shouldn't predict much once you control for them. The same worry applies to your second puzzle, since you can't yet separate a change in the crib from a change in your own attention after you stopped keeping the oscilloscope list.

I see three ways forward. First, write the helper claim tomorrow as a sequence of four or five steps with the conditions on each, then mark for each of your five post-May runs which steps you saw at the bench and which you only heard about in interviews. The steps that rest only on interview reports are your weak points. Second, use the seven founders who appear in both periods as your test. For the visits where the same founder came as helper and as repair-seeker, compare outcomes within the person, which removes tenure from the comparison. That would mean adding post-May fieldnotes for those seven, which you already plan. Third, keep the design as it is and name the helper claim as a working hypothesis from the pilot, with the tenure and period confound stated as a scope condition. That is a legitimate choice if you're ready to say in the paper that the pilot can't separate role from the identity of the founders. Which of the three fits what your supervisor expects at this stage?

i'm a third-year phd student, and i've spent two days a week for the past eight months at a desk in a deep-tech incubator, where founders from different ventures share a tool workshop that everyone calls the tool crib. they queue, borrow tools, fix each other's kit and talk, and a surprising number of the useful leads that founders have told me about started at that bench. i'm interested in serendipity, and in particular in the way that founders notice a chance encounter and then act on it. the crib gives me a small, bounded place where i can watch those encounters happen or fail to happen.
i draw on the serendipity literature, which treats chance as something that organisations can make more or less likely and that takes work to use, and on the work on incubators and accelerators that design the contact between founders. merton and barber 2004 cunha, clegg and mendonça 2010 dew 2009 de rond 2014 busch 2024 cohen, bingham and hallen 2019
